title: Is there a bot that trades from your own wallet, with no API keys and a permission you can revoke yourself? I came up empty.
author: rushapoil
selftext:
By "this way" I mean these four together, not one or two of them:

- it trades on-chain from the wallet you already hold, so there is no deposit and no exchange account
- no API keys anywhere in the loop
- the permission you sign is capped, and you can revoke it yourself without asking anyone
- every fill is a transaction on a public chain, so the record is not the bot's own screen

Plenty of things have one or two. "Non-custodial" gets used loosely enough that it often just means the operator does not hold your exchange password, which is not the same claim at all.

Disclosure so nobody has to dig for it: I built one that works this way, which is exactly why I want to know what else is out there. I am not linking it and this is not a pitch. I have gone through the usual lists and the recommendations in the bot subs and I have not found a second one, and "I could not find it" is a much weaker statement than it sounds.

So: does one exist? If you know it, name it.

comments.author: trunksta
comments.body: No API keys? How's it going to communicate cup and string?

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
Right, that is the distinction I was reaching for. On chain there is no API key because there is no account on someone else's server to log into. The wallet owner signs one transaction granting a spending allowance to a contract, with a cap, and can revoke it later. After that an executor can call that contract to swap within the cap, and the proceeds land back on the owner's address.

So the executor is not holding the private key. What it holds is a permission, and that permission is a public object you can read and cancel from your own wallet. It is a different trust model from an API key on an exchange, where the key is the account and the venue holds the balance. Not automatically a better one, it just fails differently, and that is the part I was asking about.

replies.author: trunksta
replies.body:
It's entirely possible to do that yes

The challenge becomes this

Every chain needs its own separate set of keys
Every price feed (if fetched on chain) needs its own pool stream and calculation 

Now if you are talking about 1 single contract like you describe its trivial, and as far as approvals go yeah you just pre approve x amount which is easily revocable but that's something you'd have to constantly maintain because say you approve 10000 the second it's traded that much volume it can't go through anymore without a new approval. Good to protect against risk of losing funds, but not so good in terms of missing real setups

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
Yes, and the multi-chain part is exactly why I did not try. One chain, one contract, one pair. The price feed is not on chain either: the decision runs off chain and only the settlement is on chain, so there is no pool stream to keep alive, just a swap that either confirms or does not.

On the approval you have named the real cost, and I am not going to pretend it away. The allowance decrements on every transferFrom, so it burns down with cumulative volume, not with position size. Cycle the same capital enough times and you hit the ceiling with the money still sitting right there. That is maintenance, and a ceiling reached at the wrong hour is a setup you do not take.

I decided I would rather pay that than the alternative. An allowance that never runs out is a permission you granted once and stopped thinking about, and the ones that hurt people are the ones nobody ever revisits. A ceiling that has to be renewed is the owner saying yes a second time, from their own wallet, with the previous period's fills already on chain to look at before they do. The maintenance is the consent. I would rather run something that has to come back and ask.

replies.author: trunksta
replies.body: If you are trading directly on chain on a specific pool you should absolutely be getting your price feed from that specific pool not another proxy

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
Fair on the feed: the price that ends up mattering is the pool's own, because that is where the swap settles. Whatever a signal says beforehand, the fill is priced by the pool it lands in, and that fill sits on chain afterwards for anyone to recompute.

The circuit breaker is a good instrument and I would not argue against it, but it answers a different question than the allowance does. A drawdown breaker is code I write and I run. It protects the owner from the bot having a bad day, and it is only ever as good as the process that is supposed to trip it. The allowance ceiling is not mine at all. It is enforced by the token contract, and the owner can cut it from their own wallet without asking me first. One of those is me promising to stop. The other is them not needing my promise.

And yes, I trust it, my own money is in it, that is why it exists at all. That is not really the point though. I built it so that nobody else has to take my word for anything, and a limit that holds only because I am well behaved is exactly the kind I did not want to ship. The ceiling costs me setups. It buys the owner the ability to stop me without me.

replies.author: trunksta
replies.body: I guess it depends how much volume it's doing and how often you have to re approve. If it's relatively low frequency it might be fine. But don't forget this could not only cost valuable entries but prevent exits as well and that's a real flaw worth accounting for

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
Fair, and you are right that it is not only entries. A cap that runs out stops the sell side too, and a missed exit is worse than a missed entry. Worth being precise about who is stuck though: the cap is on my permission, not on the owner. Their coins are in their own wallet and they hold the key, so they can open any DEX and close the position themselves in the time it takes to sign. When the allowance runs out, the thing that stops is me.

On the key, that part is not how it works, and it is the bit I would most want to clear up. I never see a private key and I never ask for one. What the owner signs is a token allowance: permission for a contract they can read to spend a capped amount of one token. The bot signs with its own key, and what that key can reach in their wallet is bounded by that allowance.

You are right that revoking is easy on both sides. The difference is what sits behind the revocation. Revoke an exchange API key and your coins are still on the exchange's books, so getting them out is still someone else's decision. Revoke an allowance and there is nothing left to ask for, because the position is already in the wallet you hold the key to.

comments.author: ProposalForce
comments.body: Giving a random bot access to your wallet is a quick way to get drained

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
That is the right instinct and I am not going to argue you out of it. An unlimited approval handed to a contract nobody has read is one of the most common ways people get drained, and being on chain does not fix that on its own.

What decides it is what the approval actually says: a cap you choose, one contract, and a revoke you can send yourself from the wallet without asking anyone. If any of those three is missing, your objection stands as written. That is also why I put this as a question rather than a claim, because the version worth having is the one where you can inspect the permission instead of trusting the person offering it.

comments.author: RanDumb_YouSir
comments.body: lol no that’s quite literally not how this works. To access ANYTHING on your account it’s going to require api keys

comments.author: NefariousnessOpening
comments.body:
how can you trade on a blockchain without it being public?   
I have built some systems. I usually generate the wall programmatically fund it from a treasury wallet requiring my approval and then conditions for up or down or time when met send the funds from the trading wallet to different wallet b that i sig and the trading wallet is deleted

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
You cannot, and I stopped trying to. Every fill is public, and that turned out to be the part I wanted: if the record is on the chain, nobody has to take my word for what the bot did, me included.

Your pattern answers a different question and it answers it well. A fresh wallet per run, funded from a treasury that needs your approval, swept out and discarded, keeps each run isolated and keeps the treasury out of the blast radius. That is a solid design when you are the one running the system and the one holding the keys.

The case I could not solve that way is the other one: someone who is not you, who does not run your infrastructure, and who has to decide what to trust before anything has proven itself to them. A generated wallet still has a key and somebody holds it. What I ended up with instead is that the user keeps their own wallet and their own key, the permission they sign is capped and they can revoke it themselves whenever they want, and every fill lands on a public chain where a block explorer settles the argument. Public is the cost, and it buys the one thing a dashboard cannot.

comments.author: TaxOk4676
comments.body: Our platform uses either your own wallet (bring your own key) or you can create a wallet. Both options store the keys in an Azure KeyVault for trading signatures.
